title: The index is a real file — open it and look
summary: Stop treating the staging area as an abstraction. It is .git/index, it lists paths with blob hashes and modes, and you can write to it directly without any file on disk.
mental_model: The index is a sorted list of (mode, blob hash, path). `git add` hashes a file into the object store and writes one of these rows. A commit is that list turned into a tree. Nothing else is going on.

steps.title: Read the index as a table
steps.why: `ls-files -s` prints the actual rows: mode, blob hash, stage number, path. 100644 is a normal file, 100755 is executable. Stage 0 means 'no conflict'.
steps.expect: Two rows, and an `index` file sitting in .git.

steps.title: Prove the hash is just content
steps.why: `hash-object` computes the id git would store for that content. It matches the row in the index exactly, because that is where the row's hash came from.
steps.expect: The same 40-character hash in both, and cat-file prints the content back.

steps.title: Change the index without touching any file
steps.why: Hash some content straight into the object store with `-w`, then point the index row at it. app.py on disk is untouched — you have staged a version of the file that has never existed as a file.
steps.expect: A hash printed. The object now exists in .git/objects.

steps.title: Point the index row at that object
steps.why: `update-index --cacheinfo` writes a row by hand: mode, hash, path. Status now reports app.py as staged-and-modified, because the index disagrees with both HEAD and the disk.
steps.expect: The staged diff shows content that is nowhere on disk.

verify.label: the index holds content that exists in no file

steps.title: Turn the index into a tree
steps.why: `write-tree` is literally what `git commit` calls. It takes the index rows and produces a tree object — the thing a commit points at. Read it back with cat-file and you see the same list.
steps.expect: A tree object listing both paths with their modes and hashes.

steps.title: Put everything back
steps.why: `git restore --staged` rewrites the row from HEAD. The hand-made object stays in the database, unreferenced, until garbage collection removes it.

verify.label: the index is back to normal

steps.title: Why the file mode row matters
steps.why: Git stores exactly two file modes: 100644 and 100755. That is the entire permission model — and `update-index --chmod` is how you fix a script that lost its executable bit on a Windows checkout.
steps.expect: run.sh's mode flips to 100755 in the index.

verify.label: the executable bit is set in the index
run.sh is marked executable in the index
app.py is a normal file — git only has these two modes
the index row for app.py points back at the real content
verify.hint: git restore --staged app.py to undo the hand-written row

verify.label: the index has exactly the two tracked paths

pitfalls: `.git/index` is a binary file. Never edit it by hand — use the plumbing commands, which is what they are for.
Deleting `.git/index` is recoverable: `git reset` rebuilds it from HEAD. You lose staged-but-uncommitted work only.
Git tracks no permissions beyond the executable bit. Owner, group and read-only flags do not survive a clone.
`update-index --assume-unchanged` is often suggested for ignoring local config edits. It lies to git and causes lost changes — use a separate untracked file instead.
